result: Choanoflagellates are the closest living relatives of animals and express diverse genes required for animal multicellularity (C-type lectins, cadherins, tyrosine kinases), which predate the origin of animals.
evaluation: Claims C1-C3 are well-supported by multiple citations to published phylogenetic and genomic studies. These are established facts in the field based on prior work, not novel findings from this manuscript.

result: S. rosetta undergoes rosette development resembling early animal embryogenesis, regulated by bacterial lipids, and has a sequenced genome revealing animal gene homologs upregulated in colonies. S. rosetta can undergo sex and meiosis.
evaluation: Claims C4-C9 summarize prior work on S. rosetta biology, all supported by citations to previous studies. These establish the biological context but are not novel findings from this manuscript.

result: A forward genetic screen using EMS and X-ray mutagenesis of 15,344 clonal cultures isolated nine validated rosette defect mutants falling into seven phenotypic classes, each showing significant reduction in rosette development.
evaluation: Claims C10-C16 describe the mutagenesis screen with clear experimental data (Figure 3, Figure 3—figure supplement 1A). The scale of the screen, mutant isolation, and phenotypic classification are well-documented. This represents a major technical achievement establishing forward genetics in choanoflagellates.

result: The Rosetteless mutant (Class A) completely fails to form rosettes in the presence of ACM or live bacteria but has otherwise wild-type cell morphology and proliferation, and was isolated after EMS treatment.
evaluation: Claims C17-C19 are supported by phenotypic characterization data in Figure 3B and Figure 3—figure supplement 1B. The specificity of the rosette defect without other phenotypic abnormalities is clearly demonstrated.

result: Genome sequencing identified four Rosetteless-specific SNVs. A mapping cross with Isolate B yielded 182 haploid progeny, revealing perfect linkage (177/177) between the rosette defect and a splice donor mutation in gene EGD82922 (supercontig 8:427,804), the only coding change among the four SNVs.
evaluation: Claims C20-C29 describe the genetic mapping with strong evidence: genome sequencing data (Figure 4—figure supplement 1), successful mating cross, and perfect genetic linkage (Figure 4B). The inference that the splice donor mutation causes the phenotype (C29) is well-justified by tight linkage and absence of other candidate mutations, though complementation would strengthen this conclusion.

result: The rtls gene encodes a 119 kDa protein with signal peptide, two CTLDs containing conserved cysteines and mannose-binding motifs, serine-threonine-rich regions resembling mucin-like domains, and two internal repeat regions (RP1, RP2).
evaluation: Claims C30-C37 describe the protein structure of Rtls with clear domain analysis (Figure 5A,B,C) and appropriate citations for functional motifs. The characterization is thorough and well-supported by sequence analysis.

result: The rtlsl1 mutation (T-to-C in intron 7 splice donor) causes aberrant splicing producing multiple variant isoforms with frameshifts and early stop codons, resulting in ~25% wild-type Rtls protein levels in mutant cells.
evaluation: Claims C38-C46 are supported by RT-PCR data (Figure 5D,E) showing aberrant splice isoforms and dot blot quantification (Figure 5F) showing reduced protein levels. The molecular characterization of the mutation's effect is thorough and convincing.

result: Anti-Rtls antibody treatment significantly inhibits rosette formation (10±11% vs 88-91% in controls) without affecting cell viability or growth, demonstrating that secreted Rtls is essential and specific for rosette development.
evaluation: Claims C47-C53 are supported by antibody blocking experiments with appropriate controls (Figure 6A, Figure 6—figure supplement 1). The specificity of the effect (no growth defect, Figure 6—figure supplement 1B) strengthens the conclusion. This provides functional validation of Rtls requirement.

result: Rtls localizes to the ECM-filled center of rosettes as a thick layer at basal poles, typically connecting all but one pair of neighboring cells. This discontinuous pattern may reflect incomplete cytokinesis during rosette formation.
evaluation: Claims C54-C57 are supported by immunofluorescence data (Figure 6B,C). C58 is speculative but reasonable given the cited mechanism of rosette formation. The localization data is clear and well-documented.

result: Rtls may regulate rosette development by interacting with ECM components that fill the center of rosettes.
evaluation: C59 is explicitly a hypothesis based on Rtls localization. C60 cites prior work showing ECM in rosettes. While the hypothesis is reasonable given the data, it remains untested speculation requiring biochemical validation.

result: Rtls localization is developmentally regulated: equivalent protein levels are detected in lysates from induced and uninduced cultures, but immunofluorescence shows enrichment in rosette cores and only faint membrane-associated patches in single cells/chains (absent in mutants).
evaluation: Claims C61-C68 are supported by dot blot (Figure 5F) and immunofluorescence data (Figure 6C). C63 is speculation about why signal differs between lysates and IF, but the differential localization pattern itself is well-documented. This demonstrates developmental regulation of Rtls.

result: Rosetteless mutant cells fail to form rosettes but are otherwise wild-type, and secreted Rtls is essential for rosette development while dispensable for other life stages. The rosetteless gene is the only gene known to be required for choanoflagellate multicellular development.
evaluation: Claims C69-C71 summarize key findings supported by phenotypic characterization (C69: Figure 3B, Figure 3—figure supplement 1B), antibody blocking (C70: Figure 6A), and represent the novelty of this work (C71). These conclusions are well-supported by the data.

result: Rtls may stabilize rosette cell connections by interacting with ECM like animal lecticans, consistent with the observation that Rosetteless produces wild-type chains while rosettes differ from chains in mechanical robustness.
evaluation: C72 is speculation about Rtls function. C73 accurately describes lectican function (cited). C74 is an inference about rosette vs chain differences. While the speculation is reasonable, it remains untested and requires biochemical validation of ECM interactions.

result: Rtls CTLDs most closely resemble mannose-binding animal CTLDs (mannose binding protein, surfactant protein A) that function as pattern recognition receptors in innate immunity. Rtls may play a role in substrate recognition and cell signaling given bacterial regulation of rosette development.
evaluation: C75 is an inference from sequence similarity (Figure 5B) with citation. C76 accurately describes these proteins' functions (cited). C77 is speculation. While the sequence similarity is documented, functional similarity remains speculative without biochemical binding assays.

result: CTLD-containing proteins regulate cell adhesion and development in animals. Diverse animal genomes encode Rtls-like proteins with similar domain architecture, but whether similarities reflect homology or convergent evolution is unclear.
evaluation: C78 is supported by citations to animal CTLD functions. C79 provides specific examples with accession numbers (Figure 5—figure supplement 2). C80 acknowledges the difficulty in establishing orthology. This appropriately discusses evolutionary relationships while acknowledging uncertainty.

result: Forward genetic screens have been vital for understanding development in model organisms but restricted to limited taxa. Establishing forward genetics in choanoflagellates provides first insights into genetic underpinnings of development in these evolutionarily relevant organisms.
evaluation: C81-C82 accurately summarize the history and limitations of forward genetics (well-cited). C83 appropriately claims this work as the first forward genetic study in choanoflagellates, which is a major advance for the field.

result: S. rosetta cells have polarized morphology with apical flagellum and collar. Rosettes orient cells around a central point. S. rosetta transitions between multiple cell types and undergoes a sexual cycle with mating and meiosis.
evaluation: Claims C84-C92 describe S. rosetta biology with clear visual evidence (Figure 1). These are descriptive observations establishing the biological system, largely based on prior work (citations provided).

result: Most markers in the mapping cross followed Mendelian segregation and independent assortment, indicating S. rosetta inheritance follows classical genetics rules. The cross generated a linkage map with 27 preliminary linkage groups representing ~70% of the genome.
evaluation: Claims C93-C95 are supported by genotyping data (Figure 4—source data 1, Figure 4—figure supplement 3). The demonstration of Mendelian inheritance is important for establishing S. rosetta as a genetic model. Some segregation distortion is noted in the text but doesn't invalidate the overall conclusion.

result: Rosettes and chain colonies share some similarities (intercellular bridges, transcriptional profiles) but differ in mechanical properties: rosette connections are robust and shear-resistant while chains are fragile.
evaluation: Claims C96-C98 are supported by citations to prior work (C96) and phenotypic observations used to distinguish colony types (C97-C98). This establishes important biological distinctions between colony types.
